title: Soft Rebuild
warm:
The statement [player_name] signed for Detective Imani Brooks ran four pages, and every word of it was true except for the forty minutes she left out.

Brooks had read it twice at the steel table downtown, pen tapping, and then looked up with the particular patience of a woman who had heard ten thousand careful people tell her nine-tenths of a story. "You slept through the night of the fourteenth."

"I did."

"Your lights were on."

"I sleep with them on when he's not there."

Brooks had held her gaze a long moment. Then she had initialed the page and slid it into the folder, and [player_name] had walked out into a bright, cold afternoon with her knees shaking and the forty minutes still folded inside her like a letter she had not decided to send.

That was March. It was October now, and she and Nolan Greer were rebuilding.

It did not look the way she had imagined love looked when it finally stopped hiding. It looked like Nolan standing in her small kitchen across the hall—not his, hers—burning onions because he had decided, at forty-six, to learn to cook something without a staff. It looked like him leaving his phone face-down in another room when she spoke. It looked like a Tuesday therapist with a gray cardigan and a box of tissues [player_name] refused on principle. It looked like the private elevator chiming at three in the morning and her sitting bolt upright in bed, and Nolan waking beside her without a word, and his hand finding the small of her back and staying there until her breath came down.

He never asked what the chime meant. That was the hardest part of the rebuild, and the kindest.

Because he knew there was something. He had read her statement too—Marcus Pell had made sure of it—and Nolan Greer had not built a fortune without learning to hear the shape of what people didn't say. He knew she had given Brooks a mercy version. He knew the mercy was for him. He did not know what it had cost.

What it had cost was this:

At ten past three on the fourteenth, the elevator had chimed. [player_name], awake and restless on the couch, had gone to her peephole. Vivienne Greer had been standing in the hall in a camel raincoat, no luggage, her hair pinned the way she wore it for the lobby. Behind her, one of Pell's drivers held a single leather bag. In Vivienne's gloved hand was a thick envelope, cream, unsealed, the kind of envelope that holds money or a contract or both.

Nolan's door had been closed. It stayed closed.

Vivienne had turned—and for one terrible moment she had looked straight at [player_name]'s door, straight at the tiny glass eye, as though she knew exactly who stood behind it. She had not smiled. She had lifted the envelope an inch, the way you might lift a glass to someone across a room. Then she had walked into the elevator, and the driver followed, and the chime sounded again, and that was the last time anyone in Crownspire saw her.

Paid. That was the word the envelope said. Paid to go, or paid to stay gone, or paid by someone other than her husband—[player_name] didn't know. She only knew that telling Brooks would have hung that envelope around Nolan's neck, and she hadn't been sure it belonged there. So she had kept it. She had kept it through every rebuild dinner and every Tuesday cardigan and every three a.m. chime.

"You're somewhere else," Nolan said tonight, scraping the ruined onions into the bin.

"I'm here."

"You're here and somewhere else." He turned off the burner and leaned against her counter, sleeves pushed up, no cufflinks—she had not seen them in months. "I'm not asking. I want you to know I'm not asking."

"I know."

"But if you ever want to put it down—" He stopped. His jaw tightened; he looked at the floor, then back at her. "I would rather carry it with you than have you carry it for me. That's all. That's the whole speech. I practiced it for a week."

She laughed, and it came out wet. He crossed the kitchen and took her face in his hands, not kissing her, just holding her there, his thumbs on her cheekbones, his eyes searching hers as if he could read the forty minutes through them.

"You're not the soft alibi anymore," he said. "You know that? You're just the woman I'm trying not to lose."

The kitchen smelled like burned onion and his cologne and the rain on the window. Across the hall his penthouse stood mostly dark—he slept here more nights than not now, in her smaller bed, with her smaller view. Downstairs, Rhea Quinn's slate held no marks at all under Vivienne's name, and Brooks's folder sat in a cabinet somewhere, thick and patient, with a four-page statement in it that was true except for forty minutes.

[player_name] looked at the clock on the stove. 2:58.

She hadn't meant to stay up this late. Or maybe she had.

"Come with me," she said.

Nolan's brows drew together. "Where?"

She took his hand and led him out of her kitchen, through her front door, into the hall. The carpet was cool under her bare feet. The corridor glass at the far end held the city in cold silver. She walked him to the spot—exactly the spot, halfway between the elevator and his closed door—and stopped.

"Here," she said. "This is where she was standing."

Nolan went very still. His hand tightened around hers.

Down the shaft, faint and silver, the elevator began to rise.
